items.title: Why are some innovations from previous AI cycles forgotten about?
items.raw_excerpt: Take for example Expert Systems (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expert_system) which are AI systems designed to make logical inferences. They had systems that could do accurate logical inferences in the 1970s, and even designed a VAX chip (SID) and made medical diagnosises (MYCIN) [apparently] to a level at or above many physicians. Why are innovations like these (another example being genetic algorithms) ignored and forgotten about even though they work better in logical problems which LLMs suck at?

excerpt_i18n.en: In recent years, as artificial intelligence has gradually moved out of laboratories and into the real world, the issue of perception has returned to the center of technological discussion. From autonomous driving and smart devices to spatial intelligence and embodied intelligence, systems are no longer just about understanding information but must continuously acquire reliable signals in complex, dynamic physical environments. In practical applications, the limitations of relying solely on visual perception are increasingly exposed, prompting both academia and industry to reconsider the role of multimodal perception in the next generation of intelligent systems. Against this backdrop, wireless sensing technologies such as acoustic waves and millimeter waves are gaining attention. These technologies do not aim to "see" but instead enable devices to understand environments and behaviors by modeling and analyzing physical signals, without adding extra burden or interfering with users. While still far from widespread adoption, they are seen as a crucial foundation for supporting spatial intelligence and real-world interaction. During GAIR 2025, Zhang Jin, an associate professor at Southern University of Science and Technology, shared insights on wireless sensing, multimodal perception, and new sensing technologies for spatial intelligence. With extensive experience in related research, she focuses more on the feasibility and reliability of these technologies in real-world scenarios, rather than just their performance under experimental conditions. At the conference, AI Tech Review engaged in a dialogue with Professor Zhang Jin about wireless sensing and its applications in the real world. In the conversation, rather than offering broad judgments on the technology's prospects, she preferred to discuss the limitations and challenges faced by sensing technologies during implementation, drawing from her research practice, and shared her own remarkable personal experiences.

excerpt_i18n.en: Based on the current trend of accelerating across all sectors, the integration of AI into the health domain for ordinary people will proceed faster than anticipated, said AI researcher Li Min. Recently, Wu Jingyi, a post-2000s village doctor from Tushan Village in Jiujiang, Jiangxi, unexpectedly gained popularity online. People were not only moved by her story of taking over her grandfather's legacy as a village doctor and staying in the countryside, but also surprised by her innovative approach of using a mobile AI app to establish health records for over 200 elderly villagers, analyzing their blood pressure and pulse. Behind the viral attention to this small story is the fact that young people are beginning to use new technologies to improve the lives of the elderly. It suddenly became apparent that AI applications in health have already reached the most grassroots levels of rural areas. The mobile app used by Wu Jingyi is called "Ant Ah Fu," an AI health management application developed by Ant Group. Launched six months ago, it has surpassed 15 million monthly active users and answers over 5 million health-related questions from users daily. The development of the AI health sector goes even further. In mid-this year, Shanghai, a hub for medical excellence, saw the prestigious Ruijin Hospital suddenly announce a collaboration with Huawei to open-source a pathology large model. 01. Tech giants are entering the field, giving rise to an "AI Ah Fu" in the health sector. The "first half" of AI development focused on the intelligence limits of general large models, while the "second half" emphasizes deep scenario cultivation and practical application effectiveness in vertical sectors like law, finance, and healthcare, which are becoming the real deciding factors. According to Leiphone, since the beginning of this year, companies including overseas players like OpenAI and Google, as well as domestic firms such as Ant Group, Huawei, and Baichuan, have been rushing into the field.
excerpt_i18n.es: Según la tendencia actual de aceleración en todos los sectores, la integración de la IA en el ámbito de la salud de las personas comunes será más rápida de lo previsto, afirmó la investigadora de IA Li Min. Recientemente, Wu Jingyi, una médica rural nacida después del año 2000 de la aldea Tushan en Jiujiang, Jiangxi, se volvió inesperadamente popular en internet. Además de conmoverse por su historia de heredar el legado de su abuelo médico rural y quedarse en el campo, la gente se sorprendió por su innovador método de usar la IA en su teléfono móvil para crear archivos de salud para más de 200 ancianos de la aldea, analizando su presión arterial y pulso. Detrás de este pequeño incidente que se hizo viral, está el hecho de que los jóvenes están comenzando a utilizar nuevas tecnologías para mejorar la vida de los ancianos. De repente, todos se dieron cuenta de que la aplicación de la IA en el campo de la salud ya se ha integrado en los niveles más básicos.
